utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Hello, Mr. Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Please sit down. I just remind you that the affirmation you made to tell the truth still applies, and Ms. D'Ascoli is still asking you some questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Could the usher please verify that Mr. Krasniqi has the headphones properly because I see from here that they're not properly placed. Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I'm not receiving translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Continue, please, Ms. D'Ascoli, and we'll --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I can't hear very well, the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Now I can hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Krasniqi. Can you hear me well now?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Can you hear me well?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, now I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Good. Mr. Krasniqi, I only have some questions left for you today. Mr. Krasniqi, at pages 3 to 5 of your statement of 2000 you describe how the Serb forces, policemen, separated the women and children from men and then brought the men away, started mistreating them, asking money, maltreating them. Sir, were you amongst those men?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And at page 5 of the same statement you say that Serb forces were beating and mutilating men. Is this something you saw with your eyes?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it with my own eyes, and I heard with my own ears everything.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And can you please tell us what you saw.

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they separated us from the families and they told them to go to Albania, they separated the men from the women and said, Sit down, kneel down, like you do in the mosque and pull out everything you have in your pockets.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And in your statement you also speak about these Serb forces, these policemen, who were mutilating and beating the men who were with you.

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, they beat them. The younger ones they did beat.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. And, sir, did you also witness and see with your eyes the execution by those forces of the first group of men, the one that preceded you and that you describe at page 5 of your statement?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it with my own eyes when they killed the first group.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And who were these forces that you saw firing and killing those men?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb police, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Krasniqi, at page 4 of your statement you also speak about a Serb who had a radio handset and who was speaking into this handset. And do you remember you said --

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: You said you heard the word "execution" mentioned on the radio. Can you tell me how this Serbian man was dressed, whether he had a uniform or whether he was in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, he was not dressed in civilian clothes. No one was dressed in civilian clothes. They were policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Did he have a uniform?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were dressed in uniforms. There were no person dressed in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Could you maybe describe the uniform?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard for me to describe it, but maybe if I see it I can probably tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember the colour, for example?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If I see it, yes, but I cannot describe it in words. If you show a picture or something or a uniform, I can say it was this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: And if you look around in the courtroom, maybe -- are you able to see this colour anywhere or not?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. Where should I look?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: To any of the items --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Did you not deal with this on Friday?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Not specifically, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I told you on Friday I wasn't sure I got it right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: On Friday the witness marked a colour on a colour sheet, a pattern of uniform.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I showed you one.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move on then.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, at the end of page 8 of your statement of 2000 you say that the Serbs came back to exhume the bodies. Do you remember when was that?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they exhumed them you are asking me?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you ask the question again, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, of course. At the end of your statement, the first one of 2000, after describing the events and after describing how you participated in burying the bodies, the dead bodies that you found in your village, then you also say that the Serbs came back to exhume the bodies. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This happened on the 12th or 13th of April when they came back and pulled out the bodies, all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. And who were those Serbs, again, were they in civilian clothes or in uniforms?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't close by. I was about 1.000 metres away. There were some dressed in white clothes, some were in yellow clothes, there was a excavator and there was a truck; but I can't tell you who they were because I wasn't close. And when the sun rose, they came and pulled out, as I said, excavated all the bodies from the ground and loaded them onto the truck. They went in the direction of Rahovec.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Did you see that yourself, when they loaded the bodies on the truck?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it with my own eyes and heard everything because I was hiding in the mountain about 1.000 metres away, but I followed everything that was happening and then I saw them going in the direction of Rahovec. After that I cannot tell you more. I don't know what they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Okay. So do you know what happened to those bodies or not?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We found some of them in Rahovec, in Xerxe village, and in Prizren. In Prizren we found them in one place. They had buried them all in one single place. In Rahovec and in Xerxe they had buried them in separate graves. We found them separately. Some we didn't find at all even though ten years have passed by and we have not yet found their bodies.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: How do you know this, that the bodies were found, how do you know about these bodies found in the places that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please -- can you please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes. You said that -- you said we found these bodies in this place and in this other place, and I was asking you how you know and who found those bodies.

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The foreigners called us to go and collect the bodies. They told us that such and such a number of corpses were found in Rahovec, so we went there and collected these corpses. It was the foreigners who told us because we, ourselves, knew nothing of their whereabouts. So after that, we reburied them because before that we didn't know anything, we had no news about them, but it was because of these foreigners. And can you please raise the volume a little bit because I can't hear very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes, we will. Thank you very much, Mr. Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't have further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now it's okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. D'Ascoli. Mr. Djordjevic, it's good to see you back. Mr. Djordjevic has some questions for you, Mr. Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I just need some time to prepare for cross just in technical terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Krasniqi.

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I am Dragoljub Djordjevic, and I am the Defence counsel of the accused in this case. In an effort to learn as many details about what you have been testifying about, I will be asking you some questions bearing in mind all those things that have already been brought to my attention. I have to speak slower because of the dialect of the Albanian language that you're using. Mr. Krasniqi, when you gave one of your more recent statements it was last May. On that occasion the investigator from this Tribunal, or rather, the person that you talked to told you that this had to do with the proceedings against General Djordjevic. That's in paragraph 7 of that statement. And you verify it or authenticated the statement with your finger-print because you are illiterate. Do you remember that you were told that fact?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember this at all. I didn't recognise him, I didn't know him before. I don't remember what you are putting to me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, tell me, as a citizen of what was a common state at the time, do you know who Vlastimir Djordjevic is? You lived in the same state.

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, no. No, not at all, I didn't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now tell me, apart from this statement that you gave in May of 2008, Mr. Krasniqi, do you recall how many statements you had given before that one?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have forgotten now how many I gave. I know that I gave some statements, but I don't remember now. I know that there were foreigners who have asked me for statements, but I can't tell you how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that in July 1999, the same year when the unfortunate incident happened in Pusto Selo, that you gave a statement to the investigators from the Dutch police?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's possible, yes. 1999? Not before the event.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: After the incident and in the same year --

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before, no, I never gave any statements before what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Of course I'm asking you for the period after that. The German crime police inspector Otto took a statement from you again in 1999?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I don't think so. I don't remember that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In 1999, in June and in August, do you remember giving statements to anyone in that time-period some months after the incident -- well, you must remember that.

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, it doesn't ring any bells at all. Ten years have passed now. I can't -- I can't remember really.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, well, your memory must have been better immediately after the event than it is today, ten years after the event? Can we agree about that?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't hear very well. You can repeat your question. I thought you were not talking to me. I apologise. I apologise, really. I don't hear very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can see, Your Honour, the headphones are not put on properly, and it's no wonder that he's not hearing very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It's a problem with the head-dress. We've had it with a number of witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll be patient and I'll repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me, Mr. Krasniqi, that your memory of the events was much better in 1999 than it is today?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember about the statements you asked me about that year, I really don't remember about 1999. I don't remember. It's been a long time. I apologise, I do really.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Krasniqi. I will now be asking you some questions about the statements that you gave in light of some major discrepancies between what you said in 2008 and here at this trial, and what you said at the time when you gave those initial statements. Mere three months after the event that you describe in June, that's your first statement to a Dutch investigator, you say at page 1, paragraph 2, for all the languages: "In addition to the military units, paramilitary and police units also entered the village. I personally saw those units. Soldiers of the Serbian Army wore green camouflage uniforms, while the paramilitary units and the police units wore blue camouflage uniforms, and some special units wore black uniforms."

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not what I said. This is not what I said. The policemen who were in our village were about 30 to 40 years old. The soldiers are not of that age. Those that I saw were with police uniforms, and this is things that I went through myself, that I saw with my own eyes, and this is what I'm telling you here, things that I've seen with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely why I'm asking you this. This is what you're saying now, yet three months after the event in your statement you said the other thing. That's why I'm asking you this. How come that today you were making a completely different claim and in your statement from before you mentioned black uniforms, the military, the paramilitaries, and the police? Could you please respond.

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said, no. What you're saying is not true. Show me what I said and I will tell you -- I'm sorry to tell you this, but what you're saying is not correct. I know what I've said, and I know what I've seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'd love to show it to you but it would be to no avail because you can't read. But I referred to your statement from July 1999, page 1, paragraph 2, that's the same in all the languages and that's what it says there. That's not what I said. I read out to you what you said, what you're recorded as saying. At page 2, paragraph 3, of the same statement again in all the languages, this is what it says. Again you say, Soldiers -- soldiers, not police -- soldiers who did that wore green camouflage uniforms. And as far as I was able to see they were all above the age of 40. That's what you said today and yesterday, or rather, on Friday, and that's the only thing where you're in agreement. And that's why I thought that they were not proper soldiers but members of some Serbian paramilitary unit. Is that what you said? They were older than 40 and they belonged to a Serbian paramilitary unit?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. This is what I said, that there were no military members there, that there were these persons who were of the age 30 to 40 policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Krasniqi, didn't you say that you saw tanks in your village?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The tanks were green.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And did those tanks belong to the Yugoslav Army?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were yellow. I really don't understand you about the colours. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about the colours at all. You said yourself that the tank was green. Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We call that colour yellow. I don't know how to describe it to you in words. If you show that colour to me, I can point it out. I cannot describe the colours to you in words.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, the Defence will again move that the usher take this paper, place it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Quite some time was spent on Friday, Mr. Djordjevic, discussing two distinct problems that are relevant. First is different language descriptions of some colours from what you and I might be used to; the second is this particular witness's difficulty with observing particular colours. So you may find that what you're about to do will not help very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm fully acquainted with the witness's answers to my learned friend Ms. D'Ascoli, and I am also familiar with the extraordinary effort undertaken on her part as well as by the Bench to try to deal with this issue. I believe this will once and for all resolve the issue of colour recognition. My intention was not directed at that. I wanted to ask him something else. I wanted to say that this is D003-3234. I believe it would be useful to have it put on the ELMO, and I wanted to ask the witness to indicate the colour of the tank. If he succeeds by using this document, then I will have some follow-up questions. I won't ask him to indicate whether it's an A, B, 1, or 2, only to point at it with his finger.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, please look at the colours on the sheet of paper to your right. On that piece of paper to your right, show me the colour of the tank.

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That was the tank's colour. What is your name for that colour?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We call it "verdhe," yellow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: For the record, the witness pointed to the blue colour patch.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know how it's called, but where I come from the colour of the tank was of this colour that I showed. I don't know how it's standardly called.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what is the name for the colour on the left, upper row left?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What is your name for that colour?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We call it grass colour. This is how we call it, but I didn't see it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What about the colour in the row at the bottom to the right?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Indicates]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one is yellow. We call it "sari."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Again, for the record, Mr. Djordjevic, when the witness pointed out a grass colour it was the right upper colour patch to which he pointed, not the left upper, as you had asked.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour. I corrected myself when the witness said that by saying that it was in the upper right-hand side corner.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Concerning the first colour you indicated, next can you look at the patch in the upper row just above the first patch?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: First row?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That one.

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is red. We call it red.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This item D003-3234 I would like to seek to tender that by -- and also to add that the witness pointed out certain patches in the order recorded by the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, the red is the colour that was in the centre, upper colour patch.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D223, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is already in e-court. Perhaps I can have the hard copy back, it is D003-3234. Thank you. Your Honours, now it becomes clear what we did not understand on Friday, that is to say that the witness is not color-blind, rather, the problem is his denomination of the colours. If I may have a moment before my next question. It has to do with the vehicles used by the VJ and the police. I just need to find out the number. It is P318. Can that be shown to the witness, please, and I would like him to point out the vehicle for which he said was the tank. Perhaps he can point at it with his finger or with the pen provided to him by the usher. I think it is page 4 of P318. Perhaps he can tell me whether that is a tank. This is obviously not it. Perhaps before that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... the next photograph. I would kindly ask for the next photograph. I'm not interested in any of these vehicles. Perhaps the previous photograph, not the vehicles numbers 13, 14, and 15. I conclude that there must be several pages in P318.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you see a tank on any of these photographs, witness?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These were not the ones that were there. This one has tires.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'll move on. Was that a tracked vehicle?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it had tracks. It was yellow on tracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the photographs preceding these, that is to say photographs 8, 7, 6, and 5, I presume.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you see such a vehicle here, tank?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one here possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask the usher to provide the witness with an electronic pen so that he can mark the vehicle in whichever way he finds best.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, using the pen you hold in your hand, please mark the vehicle, touch the screen with the pen to indicate which vehicle it is.

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That is a tank? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it would be useful to look at photos 1 to 4 as well. Sheet number 2 of Exhibit P318 will be received.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D224, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think there was a misunderstanding, Your Honour. I believe you wanted the witness to see the page number 2. I do find this was sufficient, but I shall comply with your wishes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I notice the word of the witness "possibly this one," so we might as well look at the remaining ones in the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we next see the photographs before these, probably the numbers are 4, 3, 2, and 1, page 1, I suppose or page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: There, Mr. Krasniqi, more tracked vehicles.

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: These ones were not there, but on the 7th at the school these were there; whereas where the massacre was committed, these vehicles were not there. There were only the yellow ones that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Krasniqi. Thank you. I can see that we have already assigned an exhibit number. You marked in red what you believed was the tank. I can tell you that the police force did not have tanks, and all vehicles were green or the colour of grass. None of it was yellow as you called it. There was not a single tank that was dyed blue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, you're giving evidence at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course Defence is obligated to put forth such evidence to confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, in your first statement from July of 1999 I counted 32 occasions when you mentioned the word "army" and only in one place you mentioned the word "police." Ten years later it is the other way around, everything is police and there's almost no army. How do you explain that?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I'm sorry, just briefly. If my learned colleague can be more specific when he mentions statements because in saying in your first statement from July of 1999, it doesn't specify to which statement he's referring to, and I'm afraid the witness could be confused about that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness has no memory of having given a statement in July 1999, so it will be important I think for the record only to be identifying the statement. Thank you, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. It is D003-3209 of the 7 of July, 1999. Mr. Krasniqi gave that statement to the member of an investigative team of the Dutch police. It was around 10.25. That is the statement I'm referring to, and I've been referring to it throughout. I didn't mention the August statement. In that statement I counted 32 words that have to do with the army, including uniforms and soldiers, and only once did he mention the word "police." I'm asking him this: How come now, a decade later, there is such a difference in the way he describes things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know what you're saying. I don't remember a thing of the things you're saying. How am I supposed to explain something that I don't know?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, obviously you do not remember, therefore I will have to jog your memory. Your statement of the 1st of August, 1999, to Mr. Otto, who was a senior crime inspector, in -- the statement was drafted in German and translated into English, B/C/S, and Albanian. It is D003-3296, your statement of the 1st of August, 1999. Today we realised that you recognise colours, you can tell them, but your names for them are somewhat different. However, when you say that something was the colour of grass then we all know what you mean. In your statement paragraph 4 discussing the tanks --

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't remember this part at all. I don't remember saying that. I really don't know how to explain it to you. I don't remember this at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It is rather unusual that you do not remember the things you discussed immediately after the massacre and that now, ten years later, you seem to recall some things that you did not mention before. In any case, in paragraph 4 concerning the tanks you said at the end of the paragraph: "I wanted to add that the colours -- the vehicles were of olive-grey-green colour." In paragraph 3, the one preceding it, it is stated that on the hills surrounding the village you saw two tanks out of a total of eight or out of the armoured vehicles that were there to the extent you can recall. Can you explain, were there two tanks or eight tanks or two tanks and some other vehicles amounting to a total of eight?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you are putting to me. I really don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, on -- in the statement you said that on the 31st of March, 1999, that the Serbs reached the outskirts of Pusto Selo on tanks. It is in paragraph 3 --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, you have me confused now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Go on. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You mentioned a statement to Dutch investigators in July 1999 --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. Okay. Go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Then one to German on the 1st of August, 1999, and now you're mentioning apparently a third statement, the 31st of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I'm still with the August statement in German provided to Mr. Otto. I mentioned the 31st of March, 1999, as a point of reference in paragraph 3. It says the witness then said that the Serb forces on the 31st of March, 1999, reached the outskirts of Pusto Selo on tanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: -- sorry to interrupt. If my learned colleague is still referring to the same statement, I think the witness has answered several times and he has said that he doesn't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, but I think Mr. Djordjevic must be allowed to explore some material differences, putting them to the witness, and see if he can make any comment about them. That's what Mr. Djordjevic is doing. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, paragraph 3 -- well, perhaps this would be better so as to be able to deal with any doubts maybe we can have it in English. It is D003-3226. I will wait for it to appear on the screen so that we would all be able to see what it is I'm talking about. Page 2, please. Very well. Could we have the English version? We have it in B/C/S and in German as far as I can see and not all of us can read that. Some do, however, some can, but not all. The English version, please. First of all, I asked you what the olive-grey-green colour is, and that occurs in paragraph 4.

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how to describe it in words, but show me something I can show you then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Is it green, or rather, can green be also yellow or not?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are not the same. They are different of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: When I say "yellow," I mean the colour you indicated, which we call blue, but green is green. Therefore, I'm asking you this: In paragraph 4 you said that the tanks were olive-drab or olive-grey-green in colour. Today you said they were yellow or blue, as we call it.

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand what you are putting to me. The tanks that came to our village were "verdhe" as we say it. I explained it to you. Now I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you please ask the witness to speak closer to the microphone?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, do you remember being interviewed by German investigators in 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The month?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I believe it is in August 1999.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Frankly speaking, I don't recall. I remember at an earlier time I remember there was a German guy, but I think it was July when he interviewed us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And you told him about the events in your village, did you? I didn't get any translation of that answer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: He didn't say anything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you explain a little bit more, Your Honour? Because ten years have passed. Maybe you can just give me a clue as to what he asked me. Now I don't understand. I have forgotten. And because of the war, I am not so clear in my head. I have great problems so far. Sometimes I went out at night and got lost and my family had to find where I was. I feel -- I have, rather, a thick head. I don't understand. I don't remember things. The doctors are taking care of me because I have some problems in my head, but give me some clues, some hints, and maybe I can tell you what.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well. You remember, you think, talking to a German fellow, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And did you talk about the events in your village that you've been telling us about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I spoke with a German, of course I must have spoken about what happened in my village because otherwise what business did I have with a German guy? So of course I must have spoken about these events. But tell me what you want to know, and I can answer that. But I'm sure I've spoken about my own village because I cannot speak about other things that I don't know, only about the massacre in Pastasel. This I know very well and this -- about this I can tell you from A to Z.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you remember telling him about what you described as Serb units arriving at your village one day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When was that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, the statement suggests you may have said it was the 31st of March that the Serb units arrived at your village. Do you remember that happening or do you remember talking about that to the German fellow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The year?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a blank memory. I don't recall anything at all. No, no, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may. Given my long experience as a Defence counsel and thinking about human rights and humanism regarding law and legal philosophy, perhaps this might be a good moment for me to say that I don't know whether this witness is capable of giving testimony in the manner which would be acceptable for the Court, given the fact that obviously the witness is in -- of an advanced age and he has told us quite sincerely that he's sometimes losing orientation in time and space. So this would be the mental element, as we call it, or the mens rea in the commission of a crime. And when we're talking about the witness, that refers to the capability of a witness to actually testify in court. So I think that we have a big problem here which might definitely cause a lot of problems for us in future. So perhaps this might be a good time for me to table this now that we're dealing with procedural matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That's a matter of significance. There seem to be two distinct issues there, Mr. Djordjevic. One of them is what the witness now remembers and tells us about certain events; the other is what the witness may remember about telling other people, whether they be Dutch or German or whoever, in 1999. The witness is very clear that he really doesn't remember any detail of what he may have told people in 1999. On the other hand, he has spent some time on Friday and today telling us about certain events which he says he now can remember. Now, if that is his present memory, it's perfectly valid for you to test its reliability by pointing out that he may have said things that are quite different at an earlier time, and that may leave us then with a very clear understanding of the reliability of the witness's recollection today. But I don't think it's possible to say in light of all the evidence that he's presently given that he has no capacity to speak about the events as he now remembers them. So it may be valuable for you to continue just pointing out material differences between earlier statements and the present testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I am not capable of actually doing the first evaluation that you talked about, but I would like to propose, since we are now asking questions about those two statements ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I would like to propose that both statements be admitted into evidence, the first one is of the 7th of July, 1999, D003-3209, and the other one dates the 1st of August, 1999, D003-3226.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There are three ways that can be done at least, Mr. Djordjevic, one is the witness identifying those statements as statements he has made; the second is by consent of the Prosecutor that they are statements, and that may be the most practical; and the third is by calling other witnesses to say that he made those statements. At the moment, it is this witness's evidence that he doesn't remember any one of those statements. He's not a person who reads or can sign, so it is probably not much use asking him to identify the statement. Now, perhaps it is that the Prosecution will agree that both of the previous statements you've now mentioned should now be received in evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we wouldn't agree to that since the witness doesn't remember having given those statements, nor we know those statements were read back to him or not. So I would object to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as I can remember the witness said that he was aware of the German inspector, that he heard of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Two statements will be marked for identification at the present time, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this would be Exhibit D225 marked for identification and Exhibit D226 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, do you remember that in 1999 a German spoke to you? Do you remember or not?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember anything about that. Sorry, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Let me go back to the statement that you gave on the 7th of July, 1999, page 2, paragraph 3, in all the languages. You are recorded as saying -- please listen to me --

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can read it, but I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Just hear me out. You're recorded as saying: "I saw only green military vehicles," you don't say police, "I saw people in black uniforms with insignia on their sleeves. I don't know what kind of insignia they had." Is this something that you stated at any point?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly what I said. I don't think I said that. I don't understand what you're getting at. What is in these statements?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi --

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are not the statements that were given to the Tribunal. There were other statements, 2001. 2001 in July was a statement that was given to the Tribunal, but the other ones I don't know. I don't remember any earlier ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who it was that you gave the statement in 2001 and what month -- and what was the name of the investigator from the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when you used the term "paramilitary" in your statements, what did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where did I say that?

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In your statements. I said that generally speaking. You did that in all of your statements apart from the one from 2008.

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 2008 I may have said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's not the essence of my question when you said it, but what do you mean when you say "paramilitary"? What does it mean? Can you explain to me what did you mean? If you used this word, it must have a meaning, so let's hear it. What is your meaning of the word "paramilitary"?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used that word to describe the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, it's much clearer now. Since you don't remember your statements from 1999, I will now ask you something about the statement that you gave on the 14th and 16th of January, 2000; and this is the statement that you gave to the investigators of this Tribunal about the forces that entered your village, the colours of their uniforms, what they looked like, the insignia that they had, and the weapons. You said that you remembered the statements that you gave to the investigators, so that's what I'm going to be asking you about. So the statement of the 14th and the 16th of January, year 2000, page 3, paragraph 3 B/C/S; page 3, paragraph 5, in the English; and page 3 in the Albanian you say: "At that time from the direction of school in Pusto Selo about 30 to 50 Serb policemen and soldiers headed towards us. They were all wearing green camouflage uniforms," so you don't speak about yellow or blue uniforms at all. "I saw that almost all of them were older than 40, and I assume that they were all policemen in this group because of their age; however, I did not see any of them dressed in blue camouflage uniforms." So could you please explain to me how come that you said this in 2000, and today and on Friday your testimony is completely different? Your terminology regarding colours is completely clear to us.

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't really understand what you're getting at.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I would like you to answer me. I read out what you said, that they all wore green camouflage uniforms, and after that you say blue, or rather, yellow, as you want to say. How come that in 2000 you said that they wore green camouflage uniforms, and now you say that they wore blue camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't remember what I said at the time, what I said or didn't say at the time. I don't remember. If there's a difference, I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, obviously you don't remember any difference, but I'll have to really insist on it because there is a discrepancy. And let me ask you again. You said that they all wore camouflage green uniforms, and you don't mix green with any other colour in your head. You said -- you said that there were no blue camouflage uniforms there. How come that you said that at the time and now you're telling us something completely different? So to an investigator of this Tribunal, not to a German guy or a Dutch guy. That's what you said and you signed it, or rather, you authenticated the statement with your finger-print.

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe there were mistakes in my statement, there were things that I may not have understood properly. Maybe they didn't understand what I was saying about the colours in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Today we all realised that you can tell colours apart, and we understand that when you say "yellow" you actually mean blue, and we understand that when you say "green" you mean green. And that's why I don't have a dilemma here. At page 7 of B/C/S; page 8, paragraph 2, of the English statement, the same statement, you say that the Serbs came in Serb -- in trucks, tanks, and jeeps. The pictures that -- where I recognised them, I marked them with "X," and you did mark a T-55 tank that was used by the Yugoslav Army. And you said: "I have already told you that the Serbs used an ordinary green-coloured military truck and the jeep was a Pinzgauer." Now, I want to ask you again: Do you remember how many vehicles came in at all?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I'm sorry. I've forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I want to ask you in addition to the two tanks were there any other vehicles? Were there any other tanks, armoured vehicles, jeeps, trucks? Did you see anything of the sort on the eve of the massacre?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean the day before the massacre? No, they were only on that day, on the 31st of March they came to our village. There weren't any before.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: And were there any other vehicles apart from tanks? That's what I'm asking you. Apart from tanks, were there any other vehicles?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other villages -- other vehicles, but they were not in our village. I only saw the tanks there, but I don't remember whether there were others. I saw only what came to our village, but there were some in Pastasel village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a good time for us to have our technical break. It's half past 1.00, and we started at noon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We're going to have our first break now. We will resume at five minutes past 1.00. Mr. Krasniqi, a court officer will assist you during the break, and Mr. Djordjevic will continue after the break. We adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, I will move on to your statement of last year, the 21st of May, 2008. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: At page 3, paragraph 19 in all languages you say that: "The Serbian policemen did not wear face masks, but all of them kept their green camouflage-colour caps so that no one could see their eyes." Then in the next paragraph, paragraph 20, you say: "The policemen had painted faces with some black marks somewhere below the level of their eyes." Next, paragraph 21, you say: "Many of the police officers were bearded and the age of most of them was over 30 years." In the paragraph following that, paragraph 22, you say: "I saw on the back of the police officers that there was something written on it, and since I'm illiterate I learnt from my neighbours and other people that it said 'police.'" What you said in that statement, is that correct, is that true?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the way it was, and the writing on the back of the police, that's true. They had that on their backs and their hats -- and their caps were that way too.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Green camouflage, the caps were green camouflage?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Why did you say so then? That was only a year ago, on the 31st of May last year, these were your words: "They all wore green camouflage caps."

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember what I said at the time. I've forgotten. But I would say that's the way it was. They had black caps and they had painted their faces over in black so you couldn't see their faces, they were wearing masks, but they weren't camouflage -- but I couldn't get a good look at them because we were supposed to look down at the ground all the time. They said look down at the earth that is Serbian land. We were supposed to look down at the ground all the time, so I couldn't get a good look at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you just say that they had masks on their faces or did I perhaps misunderstand you? Did you just say that they had masks over their faces or did I misunderstand you?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they didn't, no they didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me why is it you said they had green camouflage caps? Why did you say so then, whereas you seem to deny it today?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I said. They did have black caps with scarves, and their faces were painted black.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I must confess that you have greatly confused me. This is something you said for the first time. I put to you what you said back then: "Members of the Serb police did not wear masks, but they all had green camouflage caps." That's what you said. Now you're telling us they had bandannas and caps and they were painted black. What is true of all of that? Could you please provide an answer, Mr. Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their caps were black. They didn't have masks, but they did have paint on their faces, but they didn't really have masks. And the caps had a visor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you describe these visor caps for me. It's not very clear to me. This is something a helmet would have, a regular motorcycle helmet would have that you put over your face to protect it and it's transparent, but what sort of caps do you have in mind? This is really confusing.

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had black caps. I don't know what else I can tell you. And they covered -- their nose was covered. You couldn't see their noses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: It seems we have a third force now wearing a third type of uniform. First we had grey and green uniforms, now we have visor caps. In any case, in that statement of the 31st of May, given to an investigator of this Tribunal last year, you say that on their backs you saw the sign "police." You never mentioned that prior to that. You said having seen different types of insignia or patches on their sleeves, but that given the situation you were in, you were unable to observe those well and hence are unable to describe them. How come now, a decade later, you mentioned for the first time having seen the sign "police" on their backs? You have never mentioned that before, quite the contrary. You said that you did not make out any of the insignia or the patches. This is in all of your statements.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Can I please have a reference for the witness mentioning different types of insignia or patches on their sleeves, a reference to either one of the statements and page number. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You want me to find that and to share it with my learned friend? In that case, I may need a moment or two. Please bear with me. I will move on and then come back to this point so as not to waste time while looking for the reference, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, your statement of the 14th of January, 2000, and the 16th of January, 2000, paragraph 11. In that statement you say that the police and soldiers all wore green camouflage uniforms and that you saw all of them being over 40. You also say that you supposed that all of them in that group were policemen because of their age. However, you did not see any of them wearing blue camouflage uniforms. "However, I did not see any of them dressed in blue camouflage uniforms." That is what you said, as not having seen any of them in blue camouflage uniforms. That was back in 2000. Your words, Mr. Krasniqi. Why are you stating something that is contrary to that now? You also signed that statement. It was read back to you. You put your finger-print on it. It's paragraph 11. That was my first question concerning this topic. Can we get an answer, please.

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I changed anything, but I don't know what they wrote. I just know how to talk. I don't know what they wrote about it in my statement, so I can't really tell. I don't know how to read and write, so I can't tell what they're writing in these statements, whether they're true or not. All I know is I'm telling the truth, and I'm not telling any lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you state this back in 2000? Can you please answer that first. They all wore green camouflage uniforms and you say you did not see any of them wearing blue camouflage uniforms as you had before. Therefore, my first question is: Did you say this or not?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You don't know. Very well. In the same paragraph 11 you say -- well, there's a sentence in the middle of the paragraph: "I suppose that they were all policemen in this group." You supposed. You also state that your presumption was based on the fact that they were all over 40. In 2008 you say that they had police signs on their backs, as you were told by a neighbour. So in 2008 you supposed they were policemen -- sorry, that was in 2000. And in 2008 you are telling us they were policemen. How did that change come about? Why didn't you say in 2000 that they had police signs on their backs? And as of that point in time we would know they were policemen, end of story.

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about -- there's 2008 and there's 2002, but I don't know what I said at the time. I don't remember what their uniforms were like. I don't know how they were armed, but if you ask me specifically about the uniforms maybe I can remember. I remember the event, what happened that night. I remember then how the police were dressed and how people were at the school and about the military vehicles that were there. For the event I can tell you -- I can tell you that they were wearing black hats and that their noses were covered over with a visor, and -- but I can't tell you all the details. But I do remember the massacre and everything -- I can tell you everything about the massacre. Now you're asking me about the years, 2000, 2008, I don't remember which year I said what, but I can tell you what happened, exactly what happened, there. That I can tell you, and I can tell you the truth about it. Whether it's 2008 or 2002, the statement, I don't know but that's not important. But what I can tell you is what happened during the event, during the massacre. I can tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, you're quite right in saying that years do not matter, but what does matter, though, are the drastic differences in your two statements. I'm only referring to the years for the sake of my learned friend, Madam Prosecutor, and not for your sake. I'm only putting to you that in one statement you said one thing, stating something quite otherwise, quite contrary to it in the next statement. Perhaps you can clarify that for me. That was my first question. My second question is this -- first, let's go back to the reference sought by Madam Prosecutor. It is the July statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Djordjevic, we've been silent until now. At any stage, but certainly with this witness, could I suggest that you keep your question to one subject and keep it short and clear. You tend to have a habit of asking a number of details, perhaps that you've read from a statement or that you suggest is different from what the witness says in his evidence and what was written in an earlier statement. The witness, when you do that, tends to answer you about the very last thing you have put to him and not about what you have said before that. I think it's going to be more satisfactory for you and your questions - it's certainly going to help us more - if you just put one question to the witness and get his answer and then move on to the next question. So if you want to know about the colour of a hat or a uniform, deal with that. If you want to know whether there was a tank or some other vehicle or several vehicles, deal with that and so on. And I think we may all make better progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right, Your Honour. It was only my modest attempt to get the witness to understand what it is that I was asking him because most of my questions were answered with "I don't know" or "I don't remember." I apologise. I will strive to be more direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, in one statement you said that they all wore green camouflage uniforms, that they had no blue uniforms whatsoever; and in the other statement you say quite the opposite. Why is that? Once you put it one way, the next time you put it the another way. Why did you change that?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what to say. I don't remember things. Maybe I may have said, but I don't remember. I don't understand any of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you why you changed your original statement from green to blue, from blue to black, perhaps you can answer that; if not, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what to say. I -- actually, I don't realise I have changed anything. This is what I'm saying. I'm only stressing that I know everything that happened in relation to the massacre. This I can testify to in every single detail. I feel very sick, you know, now; but if you want me to testify to the event, that I can do very well. That I can speak about. But what other things you are putting to me, I don't know. Maybe I've made some mistakes about what you are saying because I haven't been feeling very well. I don't remember what you are asking me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You said you felt unwell. Does that mean that I can continue or not? I don't wish to pursue any matters any further if you are not feeling well.

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you asked me about things I know, of course I can give you an answer. I can go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Your statement of the 14th of January, 2000, the last page, if we count from the bottom of the page it is the fourth paragraph from the bottom, you say: "You ask me if I'm able to recognise any shoulder patches used by the Serbs. I do not think I am able to do that. Investigator Kristiansen showed me several patches, but I did not recognise any of them." That was in 2000. In 2008 you discuss police insignia or signs on their backs. Why didn't you mention that in 2000?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I said. I know this, yes, I said, it was written "milicija."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did it say "milicija" or "policija"?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Policija," "policija."

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Why did you say that in 2008 and you never said that before, yet you were asked about the insignia before that time?

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think it's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This I don't know. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: I'm sorry --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I don't know. Maybe they didn't ask me about that. They didn't ask me this question probably. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, Ms. D'Ascoli.

utterances.speaker: MS. D'ASCOLI
utterances.text: Yes. I think it's quite two different aspects, because in the statement of 2000 we're speaking about shoulder patches that were shown to him by the investigator, while in 2008 he's just mentioning having seen something written at the back of the police officers in paragraph 22. I don't see how this could be the same event or the same fact he was asked about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No doubt that will be your submission in due course, Ms. D'Ascoli, but we're interested to hear the explanation of the witness if he is able to give one. And I think we've probably heard his explanation as best as he's offering it in that last answer, Mr. Djordjevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, Your Honour. Let us move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, can you tell us as regards 1998 and 1999 the name of your village is Pusto Selo. Were there any KLA positions around your village?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: But not in my village. There were KLA but not in my village. I don't know where. There was no KLA presence in 1998 or any time. There were only the police and the army, more army, but not KLA presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Where was there more army than the police?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1998 in Pastasel village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell me, how did you conclude that the Serbian forces that attacked you were actually the police?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: How did I conclude that? I saw them with my own eyes, and I heard what was going on. Nobody made me say this. I saw it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you how did you know whether they were the army, the police, or the paramilitaries? That's what I'm asking you.

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Everybody can distinguish the army from the uniforms, from the -- from the insignia, everybody could know that and everybody could tell the police, the milicija. Usually the army members are young people, 20, 22, 23, this I know. Police are older. And in 1998 the military behaved well. They didn't do anything wrong. They didn't kill anyone. They didn't set fire to any houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What about the reservists in the army, how old would they be? There was a state of war; have you forgotten that?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reservists might be from 25, 30 years old, but in 1998 they did little damage to us. They didn't kill us. Only few people were killed that night. The damage was small. But in 1999 in March, the entire village was destroyed. 106 were killed. The houses were all burned. Every single house was set fire to that night. This is what happened that night. But in 1998 the damage inflicted on us was slight.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying that this was a pity; it was a tragedy. We'll agree with it. We're just trying to determine who actually did it. That's the only thing that I'm trying to ascertain, Mr. Krasniqi. Let us go back -- Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know it either who did it, who gave the order, who was the commander. This I don't know. I only know that what happened happened that night when they came at about 2.00 I think, 1999; when they came there they separated the men from women and children and they ordered the women to head towards Albania. I showed you this. And they escorted the children and the women towards Albania and they ordered us to kneel, to fall on our knees, like we do when we are in the mosque and look down at the earth. This earth belongs to Serbia. And they started maltreating us --

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's what I heard, sir. Thank you very much. I've heard that, and it is a tragedy all this that happened, and I really sympathise and I'm sorry for that. But what I told you -- this is just my effort to ascertain who actually did it because probably there will be other trials, not before this Tribunal, that will be dealing with this. But I want to ask you this: You told me that you knew about the presence of the KLA soldiers, but where were they, do you know that? You don't --

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This I don't know. I know I can distinguish KLA members, but I don't know where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never knew where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, can you tell me how would you be able to recognise them?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know because I knew who they were. I could see their uniforms, their weapons; but in those events that I'm testifying to, there was not a single KLA member. Oh, no, there wasn't anyone from KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, in one of your statements, the 2000 statement, at page 6, paragraph 8 in the B/C/S; page 7, paragraph 3 in the English text, you say that you knew Hamed Krasniqi. Who is he?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is from the Drenofc, from Drenofc, about 20 -- 12 kilometres away from us. He was present at the burial ceremony on the 1st of April. He came to give us a hand in burying the corpses. He is from Drenofc village. He was dressed in civilian clothes like I am today. He came to assist us in the burial of the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: What else can you tell us about Hamed Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know more than that. I only know that he was there. He came to help us to bury these corpses. First to pull them out of the brook, and then to bury them. This is all I can tell you about him. I don't want to tell you any lies, and that he was dressed in civilian clothes and that this happened on the 1st of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: You stressed that he wore civilian clothes. Why did you stress that? Was it that he was wearing some other kind of clothes at other times?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you that when he was in KLA he was in KLA uniform, but I'm saying about the day when he came to assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was in the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was in before, but the day when he came to help us to bury the corpses he was unarmed and in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Well, do you know what he was in the KLA? Did he have some kind of a rank? Was he just an ordinary soldier or was he a commander of some sort?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not a commander. He was a soldier. He was at a point.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that for a fact, or is it something that you think?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know it. I know very well that he was a soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who was the KLA commander in that area?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no KLA commander in our village. There was no KLA and no KLA commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... asking you about. I didn't ask you about your village.

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who the commander was. I only know that he was a soldier at this point because sometimes we went to buy something there, and I know that there were some soldiers, because nobody told me who the commander was. I never asked about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how many Serbs lived around your village, in the area around your village?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were more Serbs in Rahovec, but in our village we didn't have any Serbs. Maybe there were some around the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear of any crimes committed by the KLA against the Serbs? Civilians, I'm not talking about the police or the military.

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, no, I didn't hear anything, and nobody told me anything, and I didn't see anything. I'm a working person. I don't know these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how many refugees were there in your village before the 31st of March, 1999, so that would be a day or two before?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they came that night you mean? Over 2-, 3.000. There were so many that they couldn't be accommodated in the school. They were distributed in different families. Some families hosted 30, 40 persons. So in total I would say there were 2-, 3.000 families from Kline, from all over they came to the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: But can you tell me why did all these people come to your village?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were leaving their own villages, and they said to us that the police had told them to go to Pastasel. As to who told them, this I don't know. But I only know that they came to our village, to the school, and that they were not allowed to go to Albania but were told to go to Pastasel. This is what they told us. This is what I know from their words.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how many women and children were there and how many men, what would be your estimate? If you can give us an estimate; if not ...

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were less men and more women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Why was it like that? Where were all those men?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know where the men were. I didn't know them. I'm simply telling you what the situation was like that time -- at that time, and that there were more men -- THE INTERPRETERS: More -- correction -- women.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and children than men.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking you. Mr. Krasniqi, we have to clear one thing up. In 1999 --

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, whatever I know I will tell you. I will not tell you any lies.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: In 1999 you said - that's your statement of the 1st of August, page 2, paragraph 6 - that there were 1.200 people from the village and refugees, that was a total. On the 14th of June you said at page --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The speakers are speaking at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: -- you said there were 2.000 people and now you say between 2.500 and 3.000 people. So could you please tell me what figure is correct, 1200, 2.000, or up to 3.000?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying you now, that is, they were about 2- to 3.000. Of course this is simply an estimate because I didn't count them. I have forgotten about that part of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me -- very well. That's not so important after all. Could you tell me, those women and children who were separated from the men and who were told to head to Albania, did they actually go towards Albania?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They went until Ratkova village, and there they were stopped and spent the night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: But did they go to Albania or did they go back and remain in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: After three, four days they were allowed to go but -- to Albania, but not that night. That night they spent the night in the open, in the Ratkova village. And after two or three days, they went to Albania. On the 1st, 2nd, 3rd of April the convoys of people headed towards Albania. The bus came from Prizren to Rahovec and took them to the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Krasniqi, but please tell me, you're talking about 4.200 German marks that the Serbs took. Who did they took that money from, who gave them the money?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I can tell you now. We had some money. They were sent to us from Germany, Switzerland, to build the school. When the Serbs came to our school, some came to us. That group, when it came to us, we selected two, three of us who knew Serbian better and sent them to negotiate with this group to ask them why they came to us. And they said, We are your commanders. You should lift your hands up. After that when they separated the families and ordered them to go to Albania, Tahir gave this money to Haxhi Jemini, who on his part gave the money to the policemen who put the money in his own pocket, 4.000, 2- or 400, I am not sure. Either 4.200 or 4.400, and then he walked away. Then another group came and they again asked us for money. And the person who spoke Serbian well told this second group that we gave the money to this other person. And then he said, You gave the money to this other person? Okay. I'll go and make sure that you did. If not, you'll see what will happen to you. And then he said, Yes, he verified what we told him, and then he said, Yes, what you told us is true. This is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DJORDJEVIC
utterances.text: So you said that Haxhi Jemini handed the money over to the police, the money that he received from Tahir Krasniqi?

utterances.speaker: BEQIR KRASNIQI [Resumed]
